name: Zinc for body odor

card.summary: Oral zinc is sometimes claimed to cut body odor; the sources consulted give no support for this use.
card.note: Thin evidence; zinc is established only for deficiency.

lead: Zinc for body odor refers to the idea, circulated in supplement and appearance communities, that zinc can reduce underarm and body odor and so help people smell cleaner. Zinc is an essential trace mineral; oral forms such as zinc gluconate and zinc acetate are used to treat or prevent zinc deficiency, and zinc compounds also appear in topical products. [1][2]

Body odor is attributed mainly to skin bacteria acting on apocrine sweat: Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species convert sweat compounds into smelly molecules such as butyric acid, isovaleric acid and thioalcohols. [3] Topical zinc has been studied in this setting. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in Acta Dermato-Venereologica in 2020, 30 healthy volunteers had one armpit treated with zinc oxide and the other with placebo for 13 days. Zinc oxide reduced total bacterial growth and counts of Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus hominis, and participants reported less self-perceived malodour with it than with placebo (p = 0.005). [4]
A 1977 letter in Archives of Dermatology addressed zinc sulfate and axillary perspiration odor. [5] No trial of oral zinc supplements for body odor was found.

In community discussion, oral zinc comes up occasionally in threads about armpit smell and hormones; one T Nation poster with persistent underarm odor mentioned having read about zinc in that context.[7] Reference sources do not link oral zinc to body odor, and the best-studied zinc-and-odor evidence is for zinc applied to the skin.[1][4]

angle.text: Users who want to smell fresher look to zinc as a way to reduce odor-causing bacteria. The published trial supporting this used zinc oxide applied to the armpit; online discussion of oral zinc has not been tested in comparable trials.

paras: Apocrine glands, which become active at puberty and are concentrated in the armpits, are the main contributor to body odor, and skin bacteria metabolize their secretions into odorants. Genetics, diet, health and medication also contribute. [3] Standard treatments listed include antiperspirants with aluminum chloride, deodorants, bathing and, for severe cases, surgery. [3]

Wikipedia's zinc deficiency article lists acne, eczema, dry skin and hair thinning among signs of deficiency, and says severe deficiency can dull taste and smell. [1] It does not link zinc to body odor.

Wikipedia's body odor article adds that skin flora break down compounds in sweat into odorous molecules, that Corynebacterium jeikeium is more common in men's armpits and linked to a rancid, cheese-like smell, and that Staphylococcus haemolyticus is more common in women's armpits and linked to a fruitier, onion-like smell.[3] A loss-of-function variant of the ABCC11 gene reduces odorant compounds and shrinks apocrine glands; the non-functional allele is common in East Asians (roughly 80 to 95 percent) and rare in European and African populations.[3] In one skin analysis, men who ate more fruit and vegetables had sweat described as more pleasant.[3]

Conditions linked to unusual odor include osmidrosis (bromhidrosis), which is associated with excess sweating, trimethylaminuria, which causes a fishy odor, and, as possible signs, fruity or ammonia-like odors associated with diabetes or kidney disease.[3] Treatments listed include prescription aluminum chloride antiperspirants, deodorants that reduce or mask odor, daily bathing with antibacterial soap and, in severe cases, endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy.[3]

The 2020 Acta Dermato-Venereologica trial was randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled in 30 healthy volunteers, with zinc oxide on one armpit and placebo on the other for 13 days. Zinc oxide lowered axillary bacterial counts, including Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus hominis, and volunteers rated their own malodour lower, although skin-surface pH rose. In laboratory tests, 19 Corynebacterium strains were inhibited at 400 mg/l or less.[4] A 1983 deodorant-evaluation paper in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science mentions zinc ricinoleate as an odor absorber.[6] Wikipedia lists zinc chloride among zinc compounds used in deodorants.[2]

Wikipedia describes zinc as an essential trace element, the second most abundant trace metal in humans after iron, a cofactor for many enzymes, and present in alcohol dehydrogenase; it says deficiency affects about two billion people in the developing world, with growth retardation, delayed sexual maturation and infection susceptibility in children, while excess intake may cause ataxia, lethargy and copper deficiency.[2] Zinc gluconate is listed as a dietary supplement form.[2] Wikipedia's zinc deficiency article lists acne, eczema, dry skin and hair thinning among signs of deficiency.[1]
No study found tests whether oral zinc supplementation alters underarm odor in people with normal zinc status.

Zinc appears in grooming and hormone-focused forum threads, typically as one of many supplements raised in connection with sweat smell. A T Nation poster describing an underarm odor that persisted after washing, alongside lab results with normal testosterone and low DHT and estradiol, said they had read about zinc in this context.[7] Another poster on testosterone therapy listed body odor among changes since starting treatment.[8] These are individual anecdotes and the threads are not about zinc supplementation trials.

The topical zinc oxide trial described above is the main human study found.[4] A 1977 letter in Archives of Dermatology addressed zinc sulfate and axillary perspiration odor.[5] No studies found of oral zinc supplements for body odor.

lore.intro: Zinc is raised in forum discussion of underarm odor and hormone balance as a possible fix, usually in passing.[7]

claims.believers: A T Nation poster with persistent underarm odor, who described their lab results in detail, said they had read about zinc in connection with body odor.[7]
claims.experts: No trial of oral zinc for body odor was found; the controlled evidence concerns zinc oxide applied to the armpit, which reduced axillary bacteria and self-rated malodour in 30 volunteers over 13 days.[4]

quick.overview:
Zinc is an essential mineral sold as an over-the-counter supplement. Some online discussion links it to reduced body odor.

The sources consulted do not mention zinc in connection with body odor.
quick.mechanism: Proponents' mechanism is not documented in the sources consulted. Body odor is generally attributed to bacteria acting on sweat.
quick.risks: Not assessed in the sources consulted for this use. Oral zinc is used for deficiency repletion.
